items.description:
Exploits like GhostLock (CVE-2026-43499) - a 15-year-old Linux kernel bug - grant root in memory only, for the current boot. No bootloader unlock, no flashing, no Knox trip, no data wipe: reboot and the device is bone-stock again. The trade-offs: root doesn't survive reboots, you can't flash ROMs/recoveries, and it only works on specific devices running firmware up to ~the June 2026 patch level.
[!TIP] Also check out Root Without Unlocking the Bootloader ↗ and Bootloader Mods & Temporary Root Solutions ↗

Rooting is not always possible or worth the tradeoffs. Locked bootloaders, warranty terms, banking apps, work profiles, and Play Integrity checks all argue against it. Current Android versions expose many system functions without root, and actively maintained tools cover the most common root use cases: debloating, ad blocking, app control, automation, and backups.
Staying unrooted also keeps Play Integrity in its strongest state, which banking, payment, and tap-to-pay apps rely on.

KernelSU does not replace or the boot ramdisk logic the way Magisk does. , the allowlist and permission checks run inside the kernel, and the Manager app talks to the kernel over a small IOCTL interface. That makes KernelSU stable across firmwares, but it also means module mounting is no longer part of the core: since the 3.0 line, KernelSU hands mounting to a metamodule. This guide covers compatibility, LKM and GKI installation, metamodules, app profiles, hiding, and recovery.
Compatibility is device-specific. Match your KMI (kernel module interface), firmware and security patch level rather than your Android version number.

items.description:
Can Android be rooted without unlocking the bootloader? Sometimes, but only temporarily and only on a narrow set of vulnerable device builds. GhostLock (CVE-2026-43499) can grant an in-memory root session while the bootloader remains locked; it is not a permanent replacement for bootloader unlocking.
[!TIP] Jump to Table of GhostLock projects ↗ for your device
The GhostLock bug (CVE-2026-43499), explained in plain English.
Almost every root method on this site follows the same recipe: unlock the bootloader, then flash a patched boot image. But unlocking comes with costs - a wiped phone, a tripped Knox fuse on Samsung devices, a bootloader that reports "unlocked" to banking apps. That's why the discovery of GhostLock in mid-2026 caused such a stir: for a narrow window of devices, some documented runtime chains avoid conventional bootloader unlocking and boot-image flashing.
This page explains GhostLock temporary root and lists documented projects by device and firmware.
[!TIP] The 30-second version: GhostLock is a 15-year-old bug in the Linux kernel that Android uses. The right app can trigger it to give itself root for the current boot only - no conventional bootloader unlock or boot-image flashing in the documented runtime chains. Reboot and root is gone; run the tool again to get it back. It only works on exact vulnerable device builds. Vendor fixes and kernel layout changes can make a tool incompatible; there is no universal security-patch-month cutoff.

items.description:
SUSFS is a kernel-level hiding extension for KernelSU and its variants. Where a userspace module can only lie to apps it manages to hook, SUSFS changes what the kernel itself reports: hidden paths, hidden mounts, spoofed results, spoofed kernel version strings and cleaned-up AVC audit logs. This page covers what it does, how the two halves fit together, how to get it on your device, and how to verify it actually loaded.
Requires an unlocked bootloader and root. Read the KernelSU Guide first if you have not rooted yet.
